analysis.investment_thesis: Indigo Paints is a legitimate, debt-free business with four consecutive years of profits, but at INR 838 it trades at 2.16× the Graham Number (~INR 387), P/E of 26.9×, and P/B of 3.74× — all far outside my required margin of safety. The price embeds speculative growth expectations, not proven earning power.
key_strengths: Near-zero debt (D/E 0.02) with INR 1,067 Cr equity — fortress balance sheet by my standards
Four consecutive years of positive earnings and operating cash flows, meeting my minimum track-record requirement
Interest coverage of ~58× (Operating Income INR 233 Cr vs Finance Cost INR 4 Cr) — no solvency risk
key_risks: P/E of 26.9× is nearly double my maximum of 15×; any earnings disappointment destroys capital rapidly at this multiple
P/B of 3.74× means you are paying INR 2.74 in air for every INR 1.00 of tangible assets — the classic hallmark of speculation
Net profit declined from INR 149 Cr (2024) to INR 142 Cr (2025) despite revenue growing; margin compression in a competitive paint market signals pricing power limits
red_flags: Graham Number ≈ INR 387 (√(22.5 × EPS ~29.8 × BVPS ~223.7)); current price INR 838 is a 116% premium — no margin of safety whatsoever
No dividend history provided; a company earning INR 142 Cr that returns nothing to shareholders forces the investor to rely entirely on market sentiment for returns
CWIP surged from INR 17 Cr (2024) to INR 221 Cr (2025), signalling a large unproven capex cycle; returns on this capital are speculative, not proven
analysis.detailed_analysis:
From my quantitative framework, Indigo Paints fails every primary valuation filter. The Graham Number, derived from proven EPS of ~INR 29.8 and book value per share of ~INR 223.7, yields a fair value of approximately INR 387 — the stock trades at INR 838, a 116% premium. A P/E of 26.9× and P/B of 3.74× are not the prices of a bargain; they are the prices of a popular story. Mr. Market is in one of his euphoric moods, and the disciplined investor must refuse to follow him there.

The business itself is not without merit — the balance sheet is nearly debt-free, operating cash flows have been positive for four straight years, and ROCE of 19.5% demonstrates decent capital efficiency. However, net profit actually contracted year-over-year (INR 149 Cr to INR 142 Cr) even as revenue grew 2.7%, hinting that competition from Asian Paints, Berger, and Akzo Nobel is squeezing margins. The surging CWIP of INR 221 Cr adds further capital deployment risk without any proven return. I require a significant discount to intrinsic value before committing a single rupee — this stock offers the opposite.
